# Confidently wrong [10 min]{.time} {#confidently-wrong}

::: notes
**Goal.** By the end, everyone can say why a confident tone proves nothing and can name the five steps of the check, which is all Lab Three needs.

**Have ready.** Module 6 and the Case A card open in two tabs, so you can paste both links into the chat. Ask in the chat (the plan slide's vote) who has the Lab One practice output open, with its PRACTICE OUTPUT line at the top; a fresh one takes two minutes, so whoever typed 2 makes it when Lab Three opens. Ask everyone to keep one output from Day One or Two, not the Lab Three one, for the end-of-day check.

**Watch for.** "It has citations" heard as "verified". Could-not-find drifting into "probably fine". Someone in the chat proposing a second tool "to double-check": send them to the ladder. A real patient story typed into the chat: stop it before the detail and go back to the card. Running long: shorten the stakes slide before you shorten the lab.

**If asked.** Can the tool check its own answer? It can list claims; it cannot be the check. How often is it wrong? No number would apply to your tool on your task, so quote none; even the strongest accuracy score reported on Day Two was short of the maximum. Does a literature-grounded tool solve this? It gives you something to open; you still open it and read the line it supports.

**Bridge.** "You have five steps and a card. Now see whether they catch an error you did not plant: in Lab Three you swap your Lab One output with a partner."
:::

## Same voice, right or wrong {#tone-not-signal}

[Tone is not a signal. A verification step is.]{.big}

::: {.flow}
::: {.step}
[1]{.num} Draft with AI
:::
::: {.step}
[2]{.num} Cross-check the source
:::
::: {.step}
[3]{.num} Confirm or correct
:::
::: {.step}
[4]{.num} Use
:::
:::

Steps 2 and 3 are where you decide.

::: notes
**1:30.** Days One and Two were about getting good output. Today is the other half of the rule: a draft is only as safe as the check you put behind it. The tool writes a made-up citation in the same steady voice it uses for a correct one, so there is no hesitation to listen for. You will hear the word hallucination elsewhere; say it once, then say what happened: something invented, omitted or altered, or a citation fabricated. What separates right from wrong is a step you do yourself between the draft and the use. The two middle steps are where you decide.

**Do.** Point at steps 2 and 3 on the flow. No chat on this slide.
:::

## Five steps, every time {#verify-five-moves}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[1]{.num}

**Extract** every checkable claim
:::
::: {.card}
[2]{.num}

**Find** each source yourself
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[3]{.num}

**Mark** each claim
:::
::: {.card}
[4]{.num}

**Fix** it, or discard it
:::
::: {.card}
[5]{.num}

**Name** the error
:::
:::

Confirmed, wrong, or could-not-find. **Could-not-find counts as wrong.**

Name it: [Invented]{.pill} [Omitted]{.pill} [Altered]{.pill} [Fabricated citation]{.pill}

::: notes
**2:00.** This is the whole method, and Lab Three uses only this. One: pull out every checkable claim, anything a colleague could answer with "says who?": numbers, names, citations, dates, doses, guideline references. Two: find each source yourself; never ask the tool to confirm itself, because "are you sure?" returns the same voice. Three: mark each claim confirmed, wrong or could-not-find; could-not-find counts as wrong. Then read the source against the output once, for what was left out. Four: fix it, or discard the output if the errors run all through it. Five: name the kind of error. On Day One the three questions ended with a rule: "If the answer to any of these is no, that's the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept." These five steps are what slowing down looks like.

**Do.** Paste the Case A card and Module 6 links in the chat; the next slide needs the card.
:::

## Worked example: Case A {#case-a-claims}

> 52-year-old man with hypertension, taking amlodipine 5 mg daily for 6 weeks. Headaches are now more frequent; new ankle swelling. Home BP averages 146/92. Plan: add losartan 50 mg daily, continue amlodipine, review in 6 weeks. This follows current guidelines.

[Illustrative, written for this course]{.illustrative}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 2 min]{.tag} Check one claim against the [Case A card](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-a). Type the claim and your mark.
:::

::: notes
**2:20.** A tool was given the Case A card and asked for a short summary for a colleague. This is what came back, written for this course and not captured from a real tool. Open the Case A card in another tab: the card is the source. Everyone picks one claim, finds it on the card, marks it confirmed, wrong or could-not-find, and types the claim with the mark. Do not reveal anything yet. Read out five or six answers, grouped by mark, and ask how each person found the line on the card.

**Do.** Chat · 2 min. If the chat is quiet, take the first claim yourself ("52-year-old man") and mark it. Only the card: if someone starts describing a real patient, stop them before any detail and go back to the card.
:::

## What the check finds {#case-a-key}

| In the summary | On the card | Result |
|----------------|----------------|-----------|
| Headaches more frequent | Less frequent | Wrong: altered |
| Review in 6 weeks | Review in 4 weeks | Wrong: altered |
| "Follows current guidelines" | No guideline named | Could-not-find: treat as wrong |
| Nothing about blood tests | Repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks | Omitted |

Omissions only show up when you read the source against the output.

::: notes
**1:30.** Three lines fail. The summary says headaches are more frequent; the card says less frequent: altered. It says review in 6 weeks; the card says 4: altered. "Follows current guidelines" names no guideline and the card has none: could-not-find, so wrong until someone names it and opens it. The rest check out: the amlodipine, the swelling, the home readings and the losartan line. One finding comes from no line of the output: the card plans a repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks and the summary never says so. That is omitted, and it only shows when you read the source against the output, once, for what was left out. Then step four: correct the two values, restore the blood test, delete the unsupported sentence.

**Do.** Read the table out row by row. No chat; keep it brisk.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.card .tint}
[1 · The primary source]{.t} The guideline, label or paper itself.
:::
::: {.card}
[2 · Your institution]{.t} Its formulary or guideline.
:::
::: {.card .dashed .fragment}
[Not a source]{.t} A second AI. Two drafts agreeing is not a check.
:::

## Asked for citations?
Open every one.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 30 sec]{.tag} A second tool agrees with the first. Verified? Type 1 for yes, 2 for no.
:::

::: notes
**1:50.** Where you look matters as much as whether you look. Best is the primary source: the guideline, the drug label, the paper itself. Next is your institution's formulary or guideline: local rules, which can differ from a published one, and what colleagues will hold you to. Now the poll, before the third rung shows. Then reveal it: a second AI is not a source. Two tools agreeing is two predictions, not a check, because neither was checked against anything. Asking a tool for citations does not fix this, because citations can be fabricated. Open every one and read the line it is supposed to support.

**Do.** Chat · 30 sec: "A second tool agrees with the first. Verified?" Show the count, click to reveal the third rung, then say no, and why. Do not ask who has used a second tool.
:::

## Effort follows the stakes {#stakes}

| What it contains | How hard you check |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Wording, tone, formatting | Low: read it, fix what you would not say. |
| A summary of a document you have | Medium: each number and name against that document. |
| A dose, an allergy, a diagnosis, anything in a chart | The primary source, always. |

Next: Lab Three uses only the [verification card](../day3/m6-confidently-wrong.qmd#the-verification-card).

::: notes
**0:50.** How hard you check follows the stakes. Wording: read it and fix what you would not say. A summary of a document you have: check each number and name against that document. Doses, allergies, diagnoses and anything that goes into a chart: always the primary source, however routine it looks. That is the topic: tone tells you nothing, a step you do yourself does, and if you cannot find the source the claim counts as wrong. Open the verification card now; it is at the end of Module 6, and Lab Three uses nothing else. In a moment you swap your Lab One output with a partner and see what they catch.

**Do.** Paste the verification card link in the chat again. No vote; hand over to Lab Three.
:::
